summary: Describes a TFTP option that lets the client and server negotiate a block size better matched to the network medium, instead of using the default small blocks. It is a draft standard.

plainLanguage.summary: TFTP moves a file in many small pieces. This option lets the two computers agree on a larger piece size that suits the network between them, so the file arrives sooner.

questions: how to speed up tftp transfers
what is the tftp blocksize option
what is the maximum tftp block size
subtitle: Lets a TFTP client and server agree on a larger block size than the default 512 octets, so files cross a LAN faster.

tldr.problem: TFTP sends a file in fixed 512-octet blocks, which wastes time on a LAN whose MTU is 1500 octets or more, because every block needs its own acknowledgement.
tldr.mechanism: The client adds a blksize option to its read or write request, and the server answers with an Option Acknowledgment (OACK) carrying a block size no larger than the one requested.
tldr.outcome: Fewer, larger blocks cut the number of packets and acknowledgements. In the RFC's own tests on a lightly loaded Ethernet, an 8192-octet block cut transfer time by 80% against 512 octets.

today: RFC 2348 is a Draft Standard. It obsoletes RFC 1783 and updates RFC 1350. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why the Default Block Size Is Slow
sections.content:
RFC 1350 defines TFTP, a simple, lock-step file transfer protocol. A client can get a file from, or put a file onto, a remote host. One of its main uses is booting diskless nodes on a local area network, and it stays popular because it is small enough to fit in a node's limited ROM.

The problem is its fixed 512-octet block size. That is not the most efficient choice on a LAN whose MTU may be 1500 octets or greater. This document adds a TFTP option, built on the option extension mechanism of RFC 2347, that lets the client and server negotiate a block size better suited to the network medium.
sections.plainLanguage: TFTP normally sends a file in 512-octet pieces. That is small for a modern LAN, and the sender must wait for a reply to every piece. This document adds a way for the two sides to agree on bigger pieces.

sections.title: The blksize Option
sections.content:
The read request or write request packet gains two extra NULL-terminated fields after the mode. The first is the option name blksize, which is case-insensitive. The second is the number of octets, written in ASCII. Valid values run from 8 to 65464 octets, inclusive.

The block size counts data octets only. It does not include the four octets of TFTP header. The RFC's example is a read request (opcode 1) for the file foobar in octet mode with a block size of 1428, which is the Ethernet MTU less the TFTP, UDP and IP header lengths.
sections.plainLanguage: The client writes a note on the request asking for a particular piece size. It may ask for anything between 8 and 65464 octets, and the number counts only the file data, not the small header.

sections.title: Accepting the Option and Ending the Transfer
sections.content:
If the server is willing, it replies with an Option Acknowledgment (OACK). The value in the OACK must be less than or equal to the value the client asked for. The client must then either use the size in the OACK or send an ERROR packet with error code 8 to end the transfer.

The rule for the final packet is unchanged from RFC 1350. A data packet shorter than the negotiated block size is the last packet. If the block size is greater than the amount of data, the first packet is the last. If the data is an exact multiple of the block size, an extra data packet with no data ends the transfer.
sections.plainLanguage: The server may agree to the size or offer a smaller one, and the client must accept that or stop. The transfer always ends with a piece that is not full, which tells both sides the file is complete.

sections.title: Measured Speedup and Security
sections.content:
The authors ran a prototype between two HP-UX 9000 machines in octet mode, on 2.25MB files over a lightly loaded Ethernet. Without a gateway, moving from 512 to 8192 octets cut the transfer time by 80%. The gain comes mostly from sending fewer packets: doubling the block size halves both the data packets and the acknowledgements, and the sender waits for an ACK half as often. A smaller effect is less per-packet framing and processing overhead.

If the block size exceeds the path MTU, IP fragmentation and reassembly add overhead, and this is more noticeable the more gateways are on the path. On security, TFTP has no mechanism and this document adds none, though the RFC states the extensions add no additional security risks.
sections.plainLanguage: Bigger pieces mean fewer trips and fewer "got it" replies, so the file arrives much faster. If a piece is too large for the network path, it must be split and reassembled, which slows things down again.
